query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of vanadium to a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will improve and stabilize its tribological performance, yielding both lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without any additional alloying elements intended to modify tribological behavior.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled vanadium additive into the CoCrFeNi matrix (e.g., at levels similar to those that have been effective in related Al-containing alloys).
generation.conditions: Sliding contact experiments carried out over a temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C, under moderate to high applied loads and typical ambient atmospheric conditions that allow oxidation processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The vanadium additive is predicted to promote a more homogenized solid solution structure (possibly favoring a bcc phase formation), reducing elemental segregation that can lead to deleterious wear mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By refining the microstructure and enhancing the hardness, vanadium reduces the propensity for adhesive and abrasive wear. At elevated temperatures, the modification may also favor the formation of lubricious surface oxide films that maintain low coefficients of friction across the wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will demonstrate consistently lower friction coefficients and significantly reduced wear rates compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, particularly maintaining these improvements as temperature increases toward 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the friction and wear performance of the unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy under the same sliding, load, and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under conditions where the sliding mechanism is influenced by both mechanical and oxidation-driven processes (i.e., room temperature to 800 °C, moderate to high loads, and standard ambient atmospheres). Extreme variations beyond these conditions or non-oxidizing environments might not yield the same benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal vanadium concentration for synergy in the CoCrFeNi matrix in the absence of aluminum; the exact phase relationships, long-term stability under cycling, and sensitivity to load variations require further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of pure CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys and another set with a small, controlled addition of vanadium. Perform sliding tribological tests over a controlled temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C at identical loads and environmental conditions. Conduct microstructural analysis (e.g., XRD, SEM) before and after testing, and measure changes in hardness, friction coefficient, and wear rate.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at various temperatures (room temperature to 800 °C)
Wear rate (mm3/Nm) for both sample sets
Microstructural changes and phase analysis (using XRD/SEM) pre-and post-testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-modified alloy does not consistently demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% improvement across the range) in both friction coefficient and wear rate, or if the microstructural modifications do not correlate with tribological improvements relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloys are of interest to many researchers due to the possibility of shaping their functional properties by, among other things, the use of alloying additives. One approach to improving the wear resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi alloy is modification through the addition of titanium. However, in this study, an alternative solution was explored by adding vanadium, which has a completely different effect on the material’s structure compared to titanium. The effect of vanadium additives on changes in the microstructure, hardness, and wear resistance of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy. The base alloys Al0.7CoCrFeNi and Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 were obtained by induction melting. The results showed that the presence of vanadium changes the microstructure of the material. In the case of the base alloy, the structure is biphasic with a visible segregation of alloying elements between phases. In contrast, the Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 alloy has a homogeneous solid solution bcc structure. The presence of vanadium increased hardness by 33%, while it significantly reduced friction wear by 73%.
